The Baker's Pantry.fact: Store flour in an airtight container in a cool, dry place to keep it fresh longer.

Measuring Up.fact: Spoon flour into the cup and level it off; scooping packs in too much.

Mixing Bowl Tools.fact: A rubber spatula scrapes every last bit of batter from the bowl.

Bread Basics.fact: Kneading builds gluten, which gives bread its stretch and chew.

The Cookie Jar.fact: Chill cookie dough for an hour so the cookies spread less in the oven.

Cake Layers.fact: Let cakes cool completely before frosting, or the icing will melt and slide.

The Pie Shop.fact: Cold butter and ice water make the flakiest pie crust.

In the Oven.fact: Give the oven time to preheat fully; many need 15 to 20 minutes.

Sweet Spices.fact: Mace and nutmeg come from the same fruit; mace is the lacy coat around the seed.

Muffin Morning.fact: Stir muffin batter just until combined; a few lumps keep muffins tender.

Sweet Sugars.fact: Keep brown sugar soft by storing it with a slice of bread in a sealed jar.

Holiday Baking.fact: Stollen is a German Christmas bread filled with dried fruit and often marzipan.

Breakfast Bakes.fact: Freeze baked scones, then warm them in the oven for a fresh-baked breakfast.

Frosting and Icing.fact: Ganache is simply chocolate melted together with warm cream.

Chocolate Lovers.fact: Cocoa beans grow inside large pods on the cacao tree.

Fruit Fillings.fact: Toss berries in a little flour before adding them so they don't all sink.

Nutty Treats.fact: Toast nuts in a dry pan for a few minutes to bring out their flavor.

Bakeware Cupboard.fact: Glass pans heat slowly; many bakers lower the oven by 25 degrees F for them.

Grandma's Recipes.fact: Copy treasured family recipe cards and keep the originals somewhere safe.

Yeast Breads.fact: Challah is a braided bread traditionally baked for the Jewish Sabbath.

Quick Breads.fact: Quick breads rise with baking soda or powder instead of yeast, so no waiting.

The Bake Sale.fact: Wrap bake sale treats one by one so buyers can grab one and go.

French Pastries.fact: Madeleines are small, shell-shaped sponge cakes from France.

Italian Treats.fact: Biscotti means twice-cooked, because the cookies are baked two times.

American Classics.fact: Boston cream pie is really a cake, filled with custard and topped with chocolate.

Cupcake Party.fact: Fill cupcake liners about two-thirds full so they rise without spilling over.

Butter and Eggs.fact: Room-temperature eggs and butter blend more smoothly into batter.

Pancakes and Waffles.fact: Flip pancakes once bubbles form on top and the edges look set.

The Little Bakeshop.fact: Many town bakers start work before dawn so bread is fresh when the doors open.

Scones and Biscuits.fact: Press a biscuit cutter straight down; twisting seals the edges and stops the rise.

Lemon Zest.fact: Zest citrus fruit before you juice it; it is much easier that way.

Candy Making.fact: A candy thermometer takes the guesswork out of fudge and caramel.

Baking Verbs.fact: To fold, gently lift and turn the batter so the air stays in.

Cheesecake.fact: A warm, wet knife cuts the cleanest cheesecake slices.

Cinnamon Rolls.fact: Slice rolled dough with unflavored dental floss for neat, round rolls.

The Donut Shop.fact: Apple fritters are fried dough studded with chunks of apple.

Gingerbread House.fact: Royal icing dries hard, which makes it the best glue for a gingerbread house.

Afternoon Tea.fact: Afternoon tea became fashionable in England in the 1840s.

Baking Science.fact: The Maillard reaction is what turns crusts golden brown and tasty.

Perfect Pie Crust.fact: Brush the crust with egg wash for a shiny, golden top.

Berry Picking.fact: Rinse berries only right before using them; moisture makes them spoil faster.

Apple Orchard.fact: Tart, firm apples like Granny Smith hold their shape well in pies.

Pumpkin Patch.fact: Use plain pumpkin puree, not pie filling, unless the recipe says otherwise.

Picnic Desserts.fact: Bar cookies travel well; cut them in the pan and pack them flat.

Kitchen Timer.fact: Set the timer for the shortest bake time in the recipe and check early.

Sourdough.fact: Sourdough rises with wild yeast and bacteria instead of store-bought yeast.

Cookie Cutters.fact: Dip cutters in flour between cuts so the dough doesn't stick.

Sprinkles and Toppings.fact: In parts of the United States, rainbow sprinkles are called jimmies.

The Breakfast Table.fact: Wrap warm muffins in a cloth napkin to keep them cozy at the table.

Fall Flavors.fact: Toss sliced apples with lemon juice to keep them from browning.

Spring Treats.fact: Rhubarb is a vegetable, but it is almost always cooked like a fruit.

Summer Desserts.fact: Pavlova was named after the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova.

Winter Warmers.fact: Day-old bread soaks up custard best for bread pudding.

Coffee Cake Corner.fact: Coffee cake is named for being served with coffee; most contain none.

Bread Shapes.fact: A boule is a round loaf; the word means ball in French.

Flour Power.fact: Bread flour has more protein than cake flour, so it makes chewier bread.

Sweet Rolls.fact: Hot cross buns are a traditional treat at Easter time.

Tarts and Tartlets.fact: Tarte Tatin is an upside-down apple tart from France.

Kitchen Helpers.fact: An oven thermometer shows whether your oven runs hot or cool.

Cookie Exchange.fact: Bake sturdy cookies for a swap; delicate ones may crumble on the way.

Custards and Puddings.fact: Creme brulee means burnt cream; its sugar top is caramelized.

Breads of the World.fact: Injera is a spongy Ethiopian flatbread made from teff flour.

The Rolling Pin.fact: Roll dough from the center outward and give it a quarter turn often.

Brownies and Bars.fact: Nanaimo bars are a no-bake treat named after a city in Canada.

Fruit Crisps.fact: Buckle, grunt and slump are all old names for homey fruit desserts.

County Fair Baking.fact: Fair judges look at taste, texture and looks, so present your best slice.

Kids in the Kitchen.fact: Let young helpers measure and stir; it teaches counting and patience.

Tropical Treats.fact: Toast shredded coconut in a dry pan until golden for extra flavor.

Maple and Honey.fact: It takes about 40 gallons of maple sap to make one gallon of syrup.

Morning Oats.fact: In Britain, a flapjack is a chewy oat bar, not a pancake.

Delicious Words.fact: For a moist cake, avoid overbaking; start checking a few minutes early.

Baking Day.fact: Read the whole recipe before you start, and set out every ingredient.

Cookies of the World.fact: Anzac biscuits are oat cookies from Australia and New Zealand.

Cake Decorating.fact: A thin crumb coat of frosting traps loose crumbs before the final layer.

Birthday Cake.fact: Birthday cakes with candles were a German custom by the late 1700s.

Wedding Cake.fact: Tall, tiered wedding cakes grew popular in Britain during the 1800s.

Pretzels and Bagels.fact: Bagels are boiled before baking, which gives them a shiny, chewy crust.

Savory Bakes.fact: Cornish pasties were a handy lunch for tin miners in England.

Herbs in Baking.fact: Rosemary and sea salt make a simple, fragrant topping for focaccia.

Seeds and Grains.fact: Caraway seeds give classic rye bread its distinctive flavor.

Oops in the Oven.fact: A cake that sinks in the middle may have had the oven door opened too soon.

Tea Time Cakes.fact: Battenberg cake has a pink and yellow checkerboard wrapped in marzipan.

Kitchen Scents.fact: Much of the smell of baking bread comes from aromas formed in the crust.

A Baker's Dozen.fact: A baker's dozen is 13; bakers once added one so no order came up short.

Chocolate Chip Cookies.fact: Brown sugar makes cookies chewier; white sugar makes them crisper.

Banana Bread.fact: Freeze overripe bananas in their peels until you are ready to bake.

Pound Cake.fact: Pound cake was named for using a pound each of butter, sugar, eggs and flour.

Strawberry Season.fact: Hull strawberries after washing them so they don't soak up water.

Cherry on Top.fact: Clafoutis is a French baked custard traditionally made with cherries.

The Bread Basket.fact: Store crusty bread in a paper or cloth bag; plastic softens the crust.

Peach Cobbler.fact: Dip peaches in boiling water for a minute and their skins slip right off.

Carrot Cake.fact: Finely grated carrots add natural sweetness and keep the cake moist.

Scottish Shortbread.fact: Classic Scottish shortbread uses only butter, sugar and flour.

The Cooling Rack.fact: Cool bakes on a wire rack so air flows underneath and bottoms stay crisp.

Marshmallow Fun.fact: Marshmallows were first made from the root of the marsh mallow plant.

Almond Delights.fact: French macarons are made with ground almonds, egg whites and sugar.

Mini Treats.fact: Mini muffins bake in about half the time of full-size ones, so check early.

Thanksgiving Table.fact: Bake pies a day ahead to free up the oven on the big day.

Bake With Love.fact: A loaf of homemade bread is a warm, welcome gift for a new neighbor.

Sweet Endings.fact: Wrap leftover cake slices tightly so they stay moist for days.
